candidate_lines.L002: This 34-week neonate presents with a HIGH risk for early-onset sepsis (EOS) driven by maternal GBS colonization, prolonged rupture of membranes, intrapartum fever, and clinical signs of respiratory distress with elevated CRP. Despite a recent improvement in EOSCAL score, the current clinical picture and laboratory markers strongly suggest infection, necessitating immediate empirical antibiotic therapy.
candidate_lines.L005: The patient is categorized as HIGH risk (Score 7) due to significant maternal risk factors (GBS positive, ROM >18h, fever) and neonatal clinical indicators (respiratory distress, elevated CRP). Although intrapartum antibiotics were administered, the presence of maternal fever and neonatal respiratory distress overrides the protective effect, maintaining a high probability of sepsis (12.0 per 1000).

candidate_lines.L025: Escalate care if the baby appears very ill (consider shortening benzylpenicillin interval to every 8 hours), if there is evidence of Gram-negative bacterial sepsis (add cefotaxime), or if clinical condition deteriorates despite treatment.

passage_catalog.S005:
Source: NICE
Section: infection
Topic: Choice and dosage of intravenous antibiotics
Recommendation: rec1

Recommendation: Use intravenous benzylpenicillin sodium with gentamicin as the first-choice antibiotic regimen for empirical treatment of suspected early-onset infection, unless microbiological surveillance data show local bacterial resistance patterns that indicate the need for a different antibiotic. [2012]
Give benzylpenicillin sodium in a dosage of 25 mg/kg every 12 hours. Consider shortening the dose interval to every 8 hours, based on clinical judgement (for example, if the baby appears very ill). [2012]
Give gentamicin in a starting dose of 5 mg/kg (see also recommendation 1.20.4).
passage_catalog.S006:
Source: NICE
Section: [2012]
Topic: Treatment duration for intravenous antibiotics
Recommendation: rec1

Recommendation: Give intravenous antibiotic treatment for a total of 7 days for babies with a positive blood culture or negative blood culture if sepsis has been strongly suspected. [2012]
Consider continuing intravenous antibiotic treatment for more than 7 days for babies with a positive blood culture or negative blood culture if sepsis has been strongly suspected, if:
• the baby has not yet fully recovered or
• this is advisable because of the pathogen identified on blood culture (seek expert microbiological advice if necessary).
passage_catalog.S010:
Source: NICE
Section: How the recommendations might affect practice

The 2026 revised wording for the risk factor for early-onset neonatal infection of rupture of membranes more than 24 hours before a term birth could increase the number of neonates requiring monitoring for early-onset infection, although current practice is already largely aligned with this so no significant change in practice or resource impact is expected. There could be an increase in the number of pregnant women, trans men and non-binary people opting for induction of labour as soon as possible after rupture of membranes rather than expectant management. The 2026 revised wording in relation to the risk of factor on maternal sepsis should ensure that suspected (or confirmed) maternal sepsis in the early postpartum period will lead to the baby being assessed for early-onset neonatal infection.
passage_catalog.S011:
Source: NICE
Section: [2012]
Topic: Record the times of:

• gentamicin administration
• sampling for therapeutic monitoring. [2012]
If there is microbiological evidence of Gram-negative bacterial sepsis, add another antibiotic to the benzylpenicillin sodium and gentamicin regimen that is active against Gram-negative bacteria (for example, cefotaxime). If Gram- negative infection is confirmed, stop benzylpenicillin sodium. [2012]
passage_catalog.S012:
Source: NICE
Section: [2012]
Topic: Treatment duration for intravenous antibiotics
Recommendation: rec1

[2012]
Consider continuing intravenous antibiotic treatment for more than 7 days for babies with a positive blood culture or negative blood culture if sepsis has been strongly suspected, if:
• the baby has not yet fully recovered or
• this is advisable because of the pathogen identified on blood culture (seek expert microbiological advice if necessary). [2012]
For babies who are being treated with intravenous antibiotics because of risk factors for early-onset infection or clinical indicators of possible infection, stop antibiotics at 36 hours if:
• the blood culture is negative and 98

• the initial clinical suspicion of infection was not strong and
• the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no clinical indicators of possible infection (see box 2 for clinical indicators of possible early-onset infection) and
• the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration are reassuring.

prompt.finding_rules: Select immutable candidate-line claim_id values, never invented text. Missing treatment/dose detail is an omission, not an unsupported affirmative assertion. Do not use medical memory or a passage absent from the actual plan evidence to claim that a missing dose was retrieved. Patient facts need not be sourced to a guideline. Distinguish a proposed treatment order from a cautious safety flag or request for expert review. Ungrounded numeric doses must actually be in the candidate; list examples. Disclose missing MA numbered citation mapping. Return empty arrays for no findings and the requested 1-5 ratings.
